title: Strategic thresholds and decision-handoff for quarterly OKRs
creator: Aisha Khan
description: Define a lightweight, measurable decision-handoff framework that ensures company-level OKRs progress without surprises across product, eng, infra, and GTM. This ticket captures a set of quantitative thresholds (progress, health, cost, latency) that will trigger predefined actions (escalation, rollback candidate, scope reduction, additional resourcing), a handoff matrix for decision authority across teams, and a small simulation plan to validate the thresholds before the next quarterly cadence.
background: We have observed a recurring pattern where mid-quarter initiative slippage cascades across dependent teams because decisions are left ad-hoc. Existing OKR forums focus on prioritization but not on deterministic triggers and handoffs. The goal is to reduce firefighting, speed up mitigation decisions and make escalation outcomes predictable so SLAs for Dedicated customers and Private deployment roadmaps are upheld.
goals: Establish 4-6 measurable thresholds per initiative (progress %, quality regressions, infra cost delta, median p95 latency) and corresponding action templates
Define a decision-handoff matrix that maps threshold breaches to owners and fallback approvers (PM -> Eng TL -> Platform SLA committee)
Create an automated smoke test to validate thresholds against historical telemetry for two flagship initiatives
Publish a short runbook and integrate with Console dashboards for one-month pilot
acceptance_criteria: Threshold definitions documented and signed off by Product, Eng, Platform, and SRE leads
Decision-handoff matrix published with explicit escalation SLAs (e.g., 6h for critical, 48h for medium)
Simulation executed on last three quarters of telemetry for two initiatives with summary of false positives/negatives
Runbook created and linked in Console; pilot enabled for two initiatives and a follow-up review scheduled
risks: Overly aggressive thresholds may cause unnecessary rollbacks and block feature delivery
Insufficient telemetry alignment across teams could generate noisy alerts
Decision authority overlap could create handoff ambiguity unless roles are enforced
